title: Conversational timing and response-position patterns
measurement_method: Same 317-row stratified sample as Phases 6 and 12. For each response, response_sentences was used to locate where (if anywhere) comic/ironic content occurs: 'start' (first sentence only), 'middle', 'end' (final sentence/clause), 'whole' (single-sentence response where the entire line is the comic unit), or 'none' (no humor detected). Rhetorical-question-opener and punchline-at-end were tagged as booleans per row. Sub-patterns requiring closer semantic judgment (self-deprecation-after-praise, sarcasm-after-obvious-statement, clarification-before-joke) were only spot-checked, not exhaustively tagged, and are flagged HYPOTHESIS rather than INFERRED.
claim_type: INFERRED for humor_position/punchline_end/rhetorical_opener/direct_answer_then_humor (systematically tagged on every sampled row); HYPOTHESIS for self_deprecation_after_praise, sarcasm_after_obvious, and clarification_before_joke (only spot-checked, insufficient systematic tagging in this pass).

humor_position_multi_sentence_only.note: Restricting to the 101/317 (31.9%) sampled responses with >1 sentence, where 'position within the response' is a meaningful question (single-sentence responses are coded 'whole' or 'none').
humor_position_multi_sentence_only.finding: INFERRED: among multi-sentence responses, humor lands at the END of the response 55.4% of the time, versus only 4.0% at the START and ~1% in the MIDDLE. This is a strong, fairly high-confidence signal (n=101) that Chandler's multi-sentence responses are structurally built to deliver a punchline last -- i.e. setup-then-punch is the dominant multi-sentence shape, not punch-then-explain.

punchline_at_end.finding: INFERRED: 63.4% of sampled responses contain some form of humor/comic framing; of those, 65.2% place the punchline/comic payoff at the final clause or sentence. Punchline-at-end is therefore the modal comic timing pattern, consistent with standard joke construction (setup precedes payoff).

rhetorical_question_as_opener.finding: INFERRED: rhetorical questions used as the response's opening or organizing move appear in roughly 5.4% of sampled responses. These cluster heavily in the 'statement_rhetorical_q' and 'disagreement_humor'/'teasing' discourse categories -- Chandler frequently opens a challenge or tease with a rhetorical question ('So being a good friend means X?') rather than a flat assertion.

structure: speaker rephrases the prior claim as an incredulous question
phrasing itself implies the answer is obviously no/absurd

direct_answer_followed_by_humor.finding: INFERRED: of the 93 sampled responses classified as containing a direct_answer, 18.3% extend that answer with a humorous clause/tag in the same response (i.e. answer-then-humor), while the remaining ~82% deliver the answer plain or extend it with something other than humor (clarification, reassurance, further factual detail). Direct-answer-then-humor is therefore a real but secondary pattern layered onto answers, not the default.

clarification_before_joke.finding: HYPOTHESIS: clarification-before-joke (a genuine clarifying question or statement followed by a comic turn within the same response) was found only once in the 317-row sample. This suggests it is a real but rare compound structure, notably rarer than joke-before-clarification or standalone clarification; not enough sampled instances to estimate a reliable dataset-wide rate beyond 'rare, plausibly 1-3% of responses'.

self_deprecation_after_praise.method_caveat: This pattern requires detecting a 'praise cue' in context_raw immediately before the response, which is a narrower semantic judgment than the primary category tags; only spot-checked rather than tagged on every sampled row, so this is HYPOTHESIS-level, not INFERRED-with-confidence like the categories above.
self_deprecation_after_praise.finding: HYPOTHESIS (low confidence, insufficient sample): the two rows spot-checked for explicit self-deprecation immediately following a compliment/praise line did not show the pattern in this sample; self-deprecating humor was frequently observed (~26 rows carried a 'protect_self' intent alongside humor, 8.2% of sample), but it was typically triggered by an awkward/vulnerable topic rather than specifically by praise. Recommend a larger, targeted re-sample filtering context_raw for praise-language (e.g. 'you're great', 'I'm proud', 'amazing') before drawing a confident conclusion on this specific sub-pattern.

sarcasm_after_obvious_statement.method_caveat: Distinguishing 'sarcasm following an obvious/redundant statement' from general observational humor requires close reading of the immediately preceding line's informational content; only tagged explicitly on 1 sampled row, with several more plausible but not systematically flagged.
sarcasm_after_obvious_statement.plausible_additional_examples_in_sample: roughly 5-10 observation_punchline rows read as reactions to a redundant/over-explained prior statement, but this was not tagged as a first-class field during classification
sarcasm_after_obvious_statement.finding: HYPOTHESIS (low confidence): sarcasm-after-obvious-statement appears to be a real but minority sub-type of the broader observation_punchline category (23.0% of sample), rather than its own dominant pattern. A dedicated re-pass explicitly flagging 'is the prior line stating something redundant/self-evident' would be needed to quantify this reliably.

opener_vs_closer_summary.finding: INFERRED: response openers are dominated by direct statements or direct answers rather than rhetorical questions (rhetorical openers are a minority pattern at 5.4%), whereas response *closers*, when humor is present at all, are dominated by the punchline (65.2%). This asymmetry supports a general 'plain-start, punchy-finish' shape for Chandler's comic responses.

length_position_interaction.note: Cross-referencing humor position with the word-count bucket used in Phase 6/12.
length_position_interaction.finding: INFERRED: 'end'-positioned humor is disproportionately a multi-sentence phenomenon (56/73 end-positioned rows, i.e. ~77%, come from multi-sentence responses), while 'whole'-positioned humor (the entire single-sentence response functions as the joke) is the modal pattern for short single-sentence responses. This is consistent with Phase 6's finding that long responses skew toward setup_punchline/disagreement_humor (multi-beat structures) while short responses skew toward direct_answer/single-beat reactions.

clearest_findings_ranked.finding: Punchline-at-end is the dominant multi-sentence humor shape: 55.4% of multi-sentence responses place the joke in the final sentence, vs ~4% at the start.
Of responses containing any humor (63.4% of sample), 65.2% deliver the punchline at the very end of the response.
Rhetorical questions as an opening/organizing move are a real but minority pattern (5.4% of sample), concentrated in challenge/tease responses.
